summary.short: Federal privacy statute for private-sector organizations: requires those collecting, using or disclosing personal information in commercial activities to follow Schedule 1 principles, including consent, access and breach reporting, enforced by the Privacy Commissioner and Federal Court. Part 1 in force from 2001-01-01; Part 2 allows electronic alternatives to paper requirements.
summary.long: Part 1 applies to organizations collecting, using or disclosing personal information in commercial activities, and to employee information of federal works, undertakings or businesses (s. 4(1)); it excludes government institutions under the Privacy Act, personal or domestic use, and journalistic, artistic or literary purposes (s. 4(2)). Organizations must comply with the Schedule 1 principles (s. 5(1)), use personal information only for purposes a reasonable person would consider appropriate (s. 5(3)), and obtain valid consent (s. 6.1) subject to exceptions (ss. 7 to 7.4). Access requests must be answered within 30 days, subject to exceptions (ss. 8, 9). Breaches of security safeguards creating a real risk of significant harm must be reported to the Commissioner and affected individuals, and breach records kept (ss. 10.1, 10.3). Individuals may complain to the Commissioner (s. 11); the Federal Court may order corrections of practices and award damages (s. 16). Knowingly contravening listed provisions or obstructing the Commissioner is an offence, with fines up to $10,000 on summary conviction or $100,000 on indictment (s. 28). Employers may not retaliate against employees who report contraventions (s. 27.1). Part 2 provides electronic alternatives where federal laws require paper. Part 1 came into force 1 January 2001 according to a note in the Act.
